meta.title: Irish A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words of Irish (Gaeilge) for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Irish has a graded examination at these levels — the Teastas Eorpach na Gaeilge (TEG) of Maynooth University — whose syllabuses describe each level but do not publish a complete word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 366 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the pronouns, question words, prepositions and little words every sentence is built out of — and the other 134 are the commonest remaining words of written Irish, counted over the articles of the Irish-language Wikipedia by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, and every spelling its initial mutations give it (bean, bhean, mbean). No subtitle frequency list exists for Irish, and an encyclopaedia's commonest words lean towards history, places and people, which is why the deck leads with the hand-written vocabulary. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 249 nouns carry their gender, which decides how the article changes them (an fear, an bhean), and show the noun with the article, its genitive and its plural (an teach, tí, tithe); the 72 verbs are headed by the imperative, the form Irish dictionaries list a verb by (déan, "do"), and show their present, past, future and verbal noun (déanann, rinne, déanfaidh, déanamh). Behind the All forms fold a verb's tenses go by person, a noun shows its lenited and eclipsed forms (theach, dteach) and a preposition its forms with a pronoun (liom, leat, leis). The spelling is the Official Standard (An Caighdeán Oifigiúil) as Wiktionary gives it. Real example sentences come with 389 of the 500 words, three apiece for 285 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; few devices have an Irish voice, so the speaker may be silent. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Irish Wikipedia (ga.wikipedia.org), its articles as of 1 November 2026, counted for this deck (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
